title: Projects
text:
As part of a white paper published by Montclair State University, two of my peers and I worked in close collaboration with the Paterson City Mayor’s Office to identify and develop solutions to an ongoing crisis in local emergency shelters. Local state law stipulates that the average length of stay in an emergency shelter must remain below a set number of days, but local shelters were not in compliance. We found that, by utilizing niche techniques ranging from merging Continuums of Care to modifying funding schemes, local emergency shelter conditions could be brought into compliance with New Jersey state law.
You can find the full chapter here: Paterson City Mayor’s Office Collaboration (PDF)






This project aims to examine how unsheltered and unhoused individuals engage in end-of-life (EoL) planning, an area that remains largely overlooked in homelessness and public health research. By drawing on survey data and semi-structured interviews, the study will explore how shelter status, geographic mobility, and access to medical and legal resources shape attitudes toward and engagement with EoL planning. By distinguishing between unsheltered individuals and those who are unhoused but mobile (e.g., living in vehicles), the research aims to highlight how mobility and fragmented service systems can disrupt continuity of care and planning at life’s end. It is my hope the findings will inform more humane and effective policies within Continuums of Care, emphasizing the importance of aligning end-of-life decisions with individual wishes rather than structural constraints.
You can find the full proposal here: Research Proposal (PDF)

The Homelessness Crisis




Individual Emergency Shelter Beds Per Homeless Individual
When looking at emergency shelter capacity relative to the homeless population, clear regional disparities emerge. States shown in red face shortages, with fewer than one shelter bed per homeless individual, while blue states indicate relatively higher capacity. This visualization highlights structural differences in how states address homelessness and emergency housing needs. The data used for this visualization was gathered from HUD data5 and a yearly report created by the World Population Review.6 Note that the map displays the contiguous United States; Alaska and Hawaii are excluded.

The Medical Debt Crisis

Medicaid Adult Coverage Expansion and Debt
In this next section I will be investigating the differences in the COVID-19 Medicaid subsidies expansion and medical debt.

















This bar chart compares medical debt collection rates across U.S. states by Medicaid expansion status in 2023, using data from Medicaid.gov7 and The Commonwealth Fund8. States are grouped by expansion status and benchmarked against the national average.
States that did not expand Medicaid show higher rates of medical debt in collections relative to both the national average and expansion states. While this does not provide causal evidence, this figure provides a quick, illustrative snapshot that highlights disparities linked to health care access and motivates deeper policy analysis.

text:
Do We Respect Our Elders?
As the average American ages, increased expenditures into elderly care have been experienced. But this raises the question, what is our care capacity and what are our healthcare outcomes?

General Population Trends
Before tackling if an elder care crisis exists, one must first ask, what have the general population trends been in the United States.









































These three plots demonstrate how the American population has been aging nearly continuously since 1850. The median age has increased from 18.9 to 39.1 years between 1850 and 2024. Further sections will investigate how an aging population has created areas of policy innovation and policy failure. For example, do we have the infrastructure to care for more elders with fewer workers? The data for these three plots were obtained from the US Decennial Census9 via the IPUMS USA database10.

section: How Does High Office Affect Wealth?
text:
How Does High Office Affect Wealth?
By virtue of studying political science, it is an inescapable truth that in our political-economic system power often acts as a wealth generation tool, and vice versa. This subsection will mostly look at wealth and power relying on public data.




My first question when thinking about how power may be translated into wealth is how individual presidents may have grown this wealth in office. While this graph may look clean and authoritative, there are several challenges that came in procuring the data. The main issue with the data is that the wealth start and end figures are calculated estimates sourced from the USOGE.11 What is interesting to see is that, at first brush, there are large percentage swings-but these largely reflect each president’s starting wealth: modest absolute gains appear enormous when starting wealth is small, while billion-dollar fortunes can swing sharply on valuation alone. Note that figures for the current administration are projections rather than final estimates.

title: Deterrence and Interstate Peace - A Logistic Analysis
text:
1.1 Research Focus
This project examines deterrence theory using state-year data from the Correlates of War (COW) 1,2,3,4 and varieties of Democracy (V-Dem)5 projects. Deterrence theory posits that States with greater military capability are less likely to be attacked and therefore less likely to experience conflict participation.6,7,8 This is closely related to Realist theories, which argue that the distribution of relative power in the international system is the primary influence on the probability of conflict.9 This produces a straightforward, testable hypothesis: as military capability increases, does the probability of interstate conflict participation decrease?
The geopolitical climate of the present moment lends the question particular urgency. Both the Russian invasion of Ukraine and the United States–Iran conflict invite scrutiny of the conditions under which military capability shapes conflict outcomes. These cases also highlight distinction this project will make: deterrence theory speaks primarily to whether capable states are attacked, not whether they initiate conflict. Hard power may not deter; rather, it may enable power projection. Especially given a sufficient motivator, such as resources, a state may logically conclude that military conflict is the rational or the optimal decision. I examine both dimensions, testing whether capability reduces conflict participation in aggregate and whether its effect differs depending on whether a state enters conflict as a defender or an aggressor.
Research Question: Does greater military capability reduce the probability that a state participates in interstate conflict?
Unit of Observation: State-year

Year ranges from 1816 to 2023.
The number of total States per year ranges from 23 to 195.

title: Deterrence and Interstate Peace - A Logistic Analysis
text:
1.2 Theoretical Framework
As stated above, deterrence theory holds that states with superior military capabilities impose prohibitively high costs on potential adversaries, thereby discouraging the initiation of conflict. The logic is relatively straightforward, a state that can credibly threaten retaliation deters rational actors from attacking. Under this view, the relationship between military capability and conflict victimization should be negative, or, more capable states should be attacked less frequently.
A competing possibility is that military capability enables offense as much as defense. States with significant hard power can project force, sustain extended campaigns, and bear the costs of conflict in ways that weaker states cannot. This creates a theoretical ambiguity in aggregated state-year data: capability may deter attacks while simultaneously enabling their initiation, potentially producing a null or even positive net relationship. This is why I break conflict down between defenders and aggressors.
The second theory examined here is the liberal peace thesis, which posits that democratic governance and economic interdependence jointly suppress conflict propensity.Trade ties raise the opportunity cost of war; democratic institutions create transparency and accountability that make conflict less attractive. These mechanisms may be mutually reinforcing meaning, the pacifying effect of trade could be stronger among democracies, where commercial interests bear more directly on policy. 10,11 I test this conditional relationship through a centered interaction term.

title: Deterrence and Interstate Peace - A Logistic Analysis
text:
1.3 Hypotheses
Primary Hypothesis (Total Deterrence):

H\(_0\): \(\beta_{\text{CINC}} = 0\)
H\(_1\): \(\beta_{\text{CINC}} < 0\)

Secondary Hypotheses (Role-Specific Deterrence):

H\(_0\): \(\beta_{\text{CINC}} = 0\) for defender status
H\(_1\): \(\beta_{\text{CINC}} < 0\) for defender status

Tertiary Hypothesis (Liberal Peace Interaction):

H\(_0\): \(\beta_{\text{Democracy} \times \text{Trade}} = 0\)
H\(_1\): \(\beta_{\text{Democracy} \times \text{Trade}} < 0\)

title: Deterrence and Interstate Peace - A Logistic Analysis
text:
2.1 Data Source
The analysis draws on the Correlates of War (COW) project, a long-running effort to systematically collect data on the history of interstate conflict. 12,13,14,15 Military capability is measured by the Composite Index of National Capability (CINC) score, a standardized index (0–1) aggregating military personnel, military expenditure, urban population, total population, iron and steel production, and energy consumption. While the CINC score in theory ranges from 0-1, no nation comes close to 1 with a maximum CINC score reported as 0.3839 and a minimum of 2^{-7}.
The second major data source is the Varieties of Democracy (V-Dem) project.16 This project measures and reports different measures of democracy, from institutional strength, to legal protections. The measure used to measure democracy is the VD1_LiberalDem variable which is an aggregated report of a countries Liberal Democracy, with 1 being a strong liberal democracy state and 0 being strong illiberal authoritarian regime.
The combined dataset spans from 1816 to 2023.

text:
2.3 Data Preparation

NOTE: The data was pre-cleaned and joined for a previous project. Please use the contact me tab and the data curration pipeline can be provided.

Several transformations are applied before estimation. Trade and population are log-transformed using log1p() to address severe right skew. log1p() (which calculates \(\ln(1+x)\)) was chosen over log(), as the data contains zeros, and tends to cluster at very low values which can cause rounding errors. Year, democracy, and log-trade are mean-centered: centering year ensures the model intercept is evaluated at the sample midpoint rather than year zero, and centering the interaction components reduces structural multicollinearity introduced by the product term.

AnalysisData <- COWData |>
  mutate(
    ConflictParticipation = ifelse(!is.na(conflict_status), 1, 0),
    IsDefender  = replace_na(ifelse(conflict_status == "Defender",  1, 0), 0),
    IsAggressor = replace_na(ifelse(conflict_status == "Aggressor", 1, 0), 0),
    LogTrade  = log1p(imports + exports),
    LogPop    = log1p(tpop),
    democracy = VD1_LiberalDem,
    YearCentered      = year      - mean(year,      na.rm = TRUE),
    LogTradeCentered  = LogTrade  - mean(LogTrade,  na.rm = TRUE),
    DemocracyCentered = democracy - mean(democracy, na.rm = TRUE)
  ) |>
  filter(!is.na(cinc), !is.na(democracy), !is.na(LogTrade))

title: Deterrence and Interstate Peace - A Logistic Analysis
text:
4.1 Model Specification
Three nested logistic regression models are estimated, progressing from a baseline to the theoretically motivated full specification:

Model 1: ConflictParticipation ~ CINC
Model 2: Model 1 + LogTrade\(_C\) + Democracy\(_C\) + LogPop + Year\(_C\)
Model 3: Model 2 + Democracy\(_C\) \(\times\) LogTrade\(_C\)

Model 3 extends Model 2 with a centered democracy × trade interaction term, testing the liberal peace proposition that trade’s conflict-reducing effect is amplified by democratic governance. An uncentered version (logitMOD3_uc) is estimated separately and used only for the VIF comparison in the diagnostics section.

CINC is positive and strongly significant across all three models. In Model 1, the bivariate log-odds coefficient is 12.04. Adding log-trade, democracy, log-population, and year in Model 2 reduces it to 5.55 - a shrinkage of roughly 54%. This attenuation indicates omitted-variable bias in the bivariate estimate: more capable states are also more populous and economically integrated, and omitting these covariates inflates the raw CINC coefficient. Even after controls, the effect remains large and positive, opposite to what deterrence theory predicts.
The full-scale odds ratio for CINC in Model 3 is 281, representing conflict odds across the entire 0–1 CINC range. No state traverses that range in practice, so a one standard deviation shift is more interpretable. With SD = 0.0321, a one-SD increase in CINC corresponds to an odds ratio of 1.2 - conflict odds rise by roughly 20% per standard deviation.
The controls behave consistently with the literature. Log-population carries a strong positive coefficient (OR \(\approx\) 1.69). Log-trade is negative (OR \(\approx\) 0.75), supporting the liberal peace claim that economic integration dampens conflict. The democracy \(\times\) trade interaction is negative (OR = 0.8711, p = 0.0259), directionally consistent with liberal peace theory, though its significance under clustering is evaluated below. However, a very surprising outcome is the democracy coefficient: 0.497. This suggests democracies may be more likely to participate in conflict. Perhaps democratic regimes are more likely to defend other democratic regimes? Again, my future work will include a measure of if a State is joining a conflict as the primary defender or aggressor, or as an ally.

text:
5.3 Brier Score and Cross-Validated AUC
The PRESS statistic, a standard OLS model comparison tool, does not apply directly to logistic regression because GLM residuals operate in log-odds space rather than in the outcome’s natural units. Two logistic-appropriate substitutes are used instead. The Brier score is the mean squared error between predicted probabilities and observed binary outcomes - it is bounded \([0, 1]\), with lower values indicating better calibration. Cross-validated AUC is estimated via five-fold cross-validation, providing an assessment that guards against overfitting.

brier <- function(model, data, outcome) {
  p <- predict(model, newdata = data, type = "response")
  y <- data[[outcome]]
  mean((y - p)^2)
}

brier1 <- round(brier(logitMOD1, AnalysisData, "ConflictParticipation"), 5)
brier2 <- round(brier(logitMOD2, AnalysisData, "ConflictParticipation"), 5)
brier3 <- round(brier(logitMOD3, AnalysisData, "ConflictParticipation"), 5)


set.seed(123)
k       <- 5
folds   <- sample(rep(1:k, length.out = nrow(AnalysisData)))
cv_aucs <- matrix(NA, nrow = k, ncol = 3)

for (i in 1:k) {
  train <- AnalysisData[folds != i, ]
  test  <- AnalysisData[folds == i, ]

  m1 <- glm(ConflictParticipation ~ cinc,
            data = train, family = binomial(link = "logit"))
  m2 <- glm(ConflictParticipation ~ cinc + LogTradeCentered + DemocracyCentered +
              LogPop + YearCentered,
            data = train, family = binomial(link = "logit"))
  m3 <- glm(ConflictParticipation ~ cinc + LogTradeCentered + DemocracyCentered +
              LogPop + YearCentered + DemocracyCentered:LogTradeCentered,
            data = train, family = binomial(link = "logit"))

  cv_aucs[i, 1] <- as.numeric(auc(roc(test$ConflictParticipation,
                     predict(m1, test, type = "response"), quiet = TRUE)))
  cv_aucs[i, 2] <- as.numeric(auc(roc(test$ConflictParticipation,
                     predict(m2, test, type = "response"), quiet = TRUE)))
  cv_aucs[i, 3] <- as.numeric(auc(roc(test$ConflictParticipation,
                     predict(m3, test, type = "response"), quiet = TRUE)))
}

title: Deterrence and Interstate Peace - A Logistic Analysis
text:
8.1 Interpretation of Findings
Contrary to deterrence theory, military capability is strongly and positively associated with conflict participation. The finding is robust across specifications, controls, and clustering. The positive CINC coefficient in the defender model is particularly notable: even when the dependent variable is restricted to being attacked, capability increases rather than decreases victimization probability. Four mechanisms may account for this pattern.
First, capability creates opportunity. Great powers can afford to pursue and sustain conflicts that weaker states cannot, and the aggressor coefficient - roughly double the defender coefficient - is consistent with this.
Second, selection effects may be at work. States that accumulate capability may have done so precisely because they are more conflict-prone, meaning observed capability proxies for strategic ambition rather than causing conflict directly.
Third, deterrence may operate at the dyadic rather than the monadic level. A positive aggregate state-year relationship does not necessarily contradict deterrence theory if capable State A deters State B while being undeterred by weaker States C and D. Dyadic analysis or network models using bterm() and the statnet family could test this directly.
Fourth, endogeneity is unresolved. States anticipating conflict invest in military capacity; observed capability may proxy for threat perception rather than shape conflict causally.

title: Deterrence and Interstate Peace - A Logistic Analysis
text:
8.2 Limitations
First, conflict occurs in only 4% of state-years. Rare events introduce bias in standard maximum likelihood logit estimation; a rare-events correction could be explored in future work. Second, endogeneity between capability and conflict is not addressed here. Third, the state-year unit aggregates over dyads, and deterrence is inherently relational. Fourth, CINC does not capture non-traditional power-projection capacity - nuclear arsenals, cyber capabilities, intelligence operations - which may be more relevant to contemporary deterrence than the composite score. Fifth, the relationship between capability and conflict may vary across historical eras; period-specific models or era interaction terms could reveal whether the post-WWII order altered these dynamics.

title: Deterrence and Interstate Peace - A Logistic Analysis
text:
8.3 Conclusion
This paper set out to test whether greater military capability reduces the probability of interstate conflict participation. Across 14,634 state-years spanning 1816–2023, the answer is clearly no. Capability is positively associated with conflict across all three outcome measures - participation, defender status, and aggressor status - and the effect survives year controls, covariate adjustment, and state-level clustering. Hard power appears to enable conflict projection at least as much as it enables deterrence. Whether this reflects opportunity, selection, the relational structure of deterrence, or some combination remains an open question well suited to future dyadic and network-based research.

Does Military Might Deter War?
Deterrence theory holds that states with greater military capability should be attacked less often, and therefore participate in conflict less often. As my graduate capstone project, I tested this proposition directly using state-year data (1816–2023) from the Correlates of War project7 and the Varieties of Democracy dataset8, estimating logistic regression models of interstate conflict participation with standard errors clustered by state. Alongside total deterrence, I separated conflict participation by role—defender versus aggressor—and tested the liberal peace thesis through a democracy × trade interaction.







Share of states participating in interstate conflict per year, 1816–2023









Conflict participation rate by military capability (CINC) quartile






The results run contrary to deterrence theory: military capability is strongly and positively associated with conflict participation, and the finding is robust across specifications, controls, and clustering. Most notably, the relationship holds even when the outcome is restricted to being attacked—more capable states are victimized more, not less—while the aggressor coefficient is roughly double the defender coefficient, consistent with capability enabling power projection rather than preventing war. The full report walks through the theoretical framework, exploratory analysis, model comparison and selection, regression diagnostics, and a discussion of mechanisms that could account for the pattern, including selection effects and dyadic-level deterrence.

Does Military Might Deter Conflict?
Full write-up: Deterrence Project (Full Project Analysis)
Deterrence theory predicts that states with greater military capability should be attacked less often, and therefore participate in less conflict. As part of my graduate coursework I tested this against 14,634 state-years spanning 1870–2014, combining the Correlates of War project’s conflict and material capabilities data12 with the Varieties of Democracy project’s liberal democracy index13. Military capability is measured by the Composite Index of National Capability (CINC), a 0–1 index aggregating military, demographic, and industrial resources. Conflict is rare-only 3.98% of state-years involve participation-which shapes every modeling decision that follows.















Every key variable shifts substantially across the two-century span. Conflict rates spike around the World Wars and decline after the Cold War, democracy rises sharply after 1990, and average capability tracks the rise and fall of major powers. These trends are why year enters every model as a control: trade alone correlates with year at r = 0.66, so without the control other predictors would absorb temporal drift.








Grouping state-years by capability quartile previews the central finding: conflict participation rises with military capability-the opposite of the deterrence prediction. States in the highest CINC quartile participated in conflict in 8.64% of state-years, versus 0.36% for the lowest quartile. Notably, the pattern holds even for defenders: more capable states are attacked more, not less.
















Testing Deterrence Formally
Three nested logistic regressions estimate conflict participation: a bivariate baseline (CINC only), a controlled specification adding log-trade, democracy, log-population, and year, and a full model adding a centered democracy × trade interaction to test the liberal peace thesis. Because the same states are observed repeatedly, standard errors are clustered by state. The likelihood ratio test favors the interaction model (χ² = 5.09, p = 0.0241) and AIC agrees (4454.1 vs 4457.2), but BIC penalizes the extra parameter (4507.3 vs 4502.8) and the interaction fails under clustering-so the simpler controlled model is preferred for inference, with the full model shown below as the most complete specification.















CINC is positive and strongly significant (z = 3.11, p = 0.00186)-the null is rejected, but in the direction opposite the deterrence prediction. The full-range odds ratio (281) is misleading since no state traverses the whole 0–1 scale; a one-standard-deviation increase in CINC corresponds to an odds ratio of 1.2. Trade is protective (OR below 1), population strongly aggravating, both consistent with the literature. Democracy and the democracy × trade interaction lose significance once within-state correlation is accounted for: the interaction is significant unclustered (p = 0.0259) but fails clustering (p = 0.333), so the liberal peace interaction is not supported here.

text:
Current Projects

Epstein Files Analysis
This ongoing project maps the social network embedded in the released Epstein corpus from the Epstein Transparency Act. A custom Python pipeline extracts email headers from tens of thousands of PDF pages, using a Mask R-CNN model to detect redactions and dual OCR engines to recover text, before a multi-pass name resolution process in R consolidates senders and recipients into a clean longitudinal network of roughly 1,000 individuals across 21 time periods. The network is then modeled using Bootstrapped Temporal Exponential Random Graph Models (BTERGM) to test two hypotheses drawn from the literature on gender and social capital. Research Questions: (1) Do ties form disproportionately between individuals of the same sex? (2) Are women more likely to occupy brokerage positions, as measured by lagged Burt’s constraint? Results support sex-based homophily in tie formation and offer weak support for the brokerage hypothesis-women exhibit marginally lower constraint (i.e., are slightly more broker-like), though the effect is small. A notable secondary finding is an asymmetric sex pattern in tie formation: men initiate fewer ties but receive more. This work was completed in collaboration with Boaz Alkalay and Elizabeth Miller. For the full analysis please use the contact me page.


Deterence Theory Analysis
This project examined deterrence theory using state-year data from the Correlates of War (COW) and Varieties of Democracy (V-Dem) projects. Deterrence theory posits that States with greater military capability are less likely to be attacked and, therefore, to participate in conflict. This is closely related to Realist theories, which argue that the distribution of relative power in the international system is the primary influence on the probability of conflict. This yields a straightforward, testable hypothesis: as military capability increases, does the probability of participation in interstate conflict decrease? Research Question: Does greater military capability reduce the probability that a state participates in interstate conflict? Modeling Tie Formation Over Time
Because ties are interdependent — an email begets a reply, shared contacts beget introductions — standard regression is inappropriate. I instead estimate a Bootstrapped Temporal Exponential Random Graph Model (btergm)4 on the 2009–2019 window, with structural controls for reciprocity, geometrically weighted degree distributions, transitive closure (GWESP), a linear time trend, and a one-year tie-memory term (R = 1,000 bootstrap resamples). H1 enters as sender- and receiver-side effects of Burt’s constraint, computed on the prior year’s network so the predictor is not endogenous to the ties being modeled; H2 enters as a same-sex match term alongside sender and receiver sex main effects. Out-of-sample tie prediction is strong (ROC AUC = 0.932 vs. a 0.51 random baseline; precision–recall AUC = 0.731 vs. 0.001), though a substantial share of that performance is carried by the memory term — persistence, not novelty, dominates elite email networks.















H1 is supported. A one-unit increase in constraint cuts the odds of receiving a tie by 74.4% (OR = 0.26, 95% CI [0.12, 0.30]) and of sending one by 71.8% (OR = 0.28, 95% CI [0.17, 0.34]) — low-constraint brokers are the network’s most active participants. H2 is supported. Same-sex dyads are 15.7% more likely to form a tie than mixed-sex dyads (OR = 1.16, 95% CI [1.10, 1.21]), net of reciprocity (OR = 176.57), popularity, transitivity, and tie persistence (memory OR = 5.09). The sex main effects reveal an unhypothesized asymmetry: male senders are 25.1% less likely to initiate a tie (OR = 0.75), while male receivers are 15.8% more likely to receive one (OR = 1.16) — women disproportionately write, men are disproportionately written to.








H1’s supplementary question — who occupies the brokerage positions? Burt’s constraint is bounded on [0, 1]: high values mean an ego’s contacts are densely interconnected (little brokerage opportunity), low values mark brokers bridging otherwise disconnected groups. Because the outcome is bounded, it is modeled with a beta regression (logit link) rather than OLS, whose residual diagnostics failed here — a specification choice that materially changed the conclusion. Controlling for year fixed effects among active nodes, men have significantly higher constraint than women (β = -0.018, 95% CI [-0.104, 0.068], z = -0.42), meaning women disproportionately occupy the broker-like positions — though the gap is modest in practical terms (about 0.02 SD).















The picture that emerges is of an elite network whose most active participants are its brokers, that clusters strongly by sex in who talks to whom, and in which women both initiate more communication and — modestly — occupy more of the structurally advantageous positions. Three caveats travel with these results: the corpus is the product of a federal investigation and is therefore an inherently selected sample of the true communication network; predictive performance leans heavily on tie persistence; and an MCMC-based mtergm robustness check proved computationally infeasible at this network size, leaving coefficient stability across bootstrap seeds as the primary robustness evidence. Full details, diagnostics, and replication materials are available upon request via the Contact Me tab.
